prompt:
A reinforcement-learning agent learns to control a simulated physical
system on a hexagonal grid. Learning works but needs tens of millions of
environment steps; the simulator is the bottleneck. Standard tricks tried:
frame skipping, prioritised replay, reward shaping, curriculum. Want a
different angle on sample efficiency.

Incorporate ideas from Laser Design and Applications (Physical Sciences > Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Laser Design and Applications) into your approach.
proposal:
## Reframing the bottleneck

"Sample efficiency" tricks (PER, reward shaping, curriculum) attack *statistical* efficiency — getting more gradient signal per transition. But if the simulator itself is the wall-clock bottleneck, the real lever is **real-step efficiency**: minimizing how often you have to touch the expensive simulator at all, and maximizing the information extracted from each touch. That's exactly the design problem laser engineers solve when getting more useful photons out of an expensive pump.

Here's a laser-engineering mapping onto that problem, from most to least load-bearing:

## 1. Cavity round-trips → world-model amplification with an explicit Q-factor

A laser doesn't emit one photon per pump event — it recirculates light through the gain medium via mirrors, extracting many stimulated-emission events per pump photon, until cavity losses balance gain. Treat a learned dynamics model as the gain medium and short real trajectory segments as the pump: each real simulator step seeds many virtual "round trips" (short model-rollout branches) that get trained on before the next real step. This is Dyna/MBPO-shaped, but the useful addition is borrowing **finesse/Q-factor as an explicit tunable**: define round-trip depth as a knob you sweep against measured model error growth per bounce, rather than a fixed hyperparameter. Below threshold (model error compounds faster than gain), cut rollout depth; above it, extend. You get a principled stopping rule instead of a guessed rollout horizon.

**Failure mode to watch, and it maps precisely:** real lasers suffer **amplified spontaneous emission (ASE)** — when the seed is too weak or the medium too greedy, the cavity amplifies its own noise instead of coherent signal, degrading beam quality. The RL analog is exactly model-bias exploitation: the policy learns to game systematic model error rather than real dynamics. The fix in both domains is the same — periodic reseeding with real data and capping gain-per-round-trip, not just capping total rollout length.

## 2. Q-switching → decouple "charging" from "release"

Q-switched lasers store pump energy in the gain medium while the cavity is deliberately lossy (closed), then dump it all at once by "opening" the cavity for a giant pulse — far higher peak power than continuous operation. Applied here: don't interleave real-simulator collection and policy updates continuously. Run long **charging phases** (pure real-data collection, or even none — just intensive world-model refinement on the existing replay buffer, zero new real steps) followed by short **Q-switched release phases** (a large burst of synthetic on-model rollouts for policy optimization). This directly minimizes real simulator touches per unit of policy improvement, and gives you a clean schedule to tune (charge duration vs. release size) instead of a continuous ratio.

## 3. Phased arrays + guide-star adaptive optics → multi-fidelity coherent combination

A phased array combines many small, cheap emitters to match a single large expensive aperture; adaptive optics uses an artificial laser guide star as a cheap synthetic reference to measure and correct wavefront distortion when a real bright star isn't available. Translate: run a swarm of **cheap, reduced-fidelity hex-grid simulators** (coarser resolution, simplified collision/contact model) in parallel — cheap per step, individually biased. Use *sparse* calls to the real high-fidelity simulator purely as a "guide star" to measure the discrepancy and fit a residual correction model, not to generate primary training data. Most learning happens off the coherently-combined cheap array; the expensive simulator's only job becomes calibration.

## 4. Heterodyne detection → learned local oscillator as control variate

Heterodyne/Doppler techniques extract a weak signal buried in noise by mixing it with a reference oscillator and reading the beat frequency — pulling SNR far above what direct measurement gives. Concretely: pair every real transition with a prediction from the learned dynamics/value model (the "local oscillator") and train on the *residual* (beat signal), not the raw return. This is control-variate/advantage estimation, but the heterodyne framing suggests being deliberate about matching timescales — separate fast per-cell hex dynamics from slow macroscopic drift and mix each down separately, so the learning signal isolates exactly the residual that's actually hard to predict, rather than re-learning already-modeled dynamics from noisy raw returns.

## 5. Chirped pulse amplification → stretch-then-compress for risky regions

CPA stretches a pulse in time (lowering peak power) before amplifying to avoid damaging the gain medium, then recompresses. For hex-grid regions that are dynamically stiff or dangerous (near obstacles/boundaries), temporally "stretch" data collection there — finer sub-stepping or slowed dynamics — to get a safer, higher-quality signal per expensive step, then reweight/recompress during off-policy training to recover the correct effective policy for full-speed operation. This differs from curriculum (which reorders *what* task difficulty you train on) by instead reshaping *how densely you sample time* within a fixed hard region.

## Suggested combined architecture

The single highest-leverage change is #1+#2 together: a learned world model as gain medium, explicit Q-factor tuning on rollout depth via measured model error, and a Q-switched charge/release schedule to structure when the real simulator gets touched at all. That's the core lever on "simulator is the bottleneck." Layer #3 in if you can build a coarse hex-grid approximation cheaply (likely, on a discrete grid). Add #4 as a training-signal quality booster once the model-based loop is stable — it's orthogonal and stacks cleanly. #5 is worth prototyping only if a specific sub-region of the grid is known to be both hard and cheap to sub-step.

Want me to sketch the Q-switch scheduler (charge/release trigger logic) or the model-error-vs-rollout-depth diagnostic for #1 in more concrete pseudocode?
